Whom, exactly, did Sohrawardî have in mind when he spoke of the Ishrâqîyûn, the “Eastern” philosophers or theosophers? The only fully satisfying answer must come from Sohrawardî’s writings taken as a whole, and from the mystical idea of the “Orient” that emerges from them.

But we should first ask whether this name was unknown before his time. In fact it was not entirely unknown; we can find traces of it. One brief and curious indication appears in a context that helps explain the reverence with which Sohrawardî brings together the names of Hermes and Zarathustra, or Zoroaster. Islam has a long Hermetic tradition, and Sohrawardî’s undertaking to “revive” the wisdom of the ancient Persians also belongs within it.

Moreover, traces of “Eastern” philosophers can be found in his illustrious predecessor Avicenna. Sohrawardî himself offered explanations of this that we must keep in mind, for they reveal the spiritual ancestry he claimed for himself and, through him, for the Ishrâqîyûn—the name by which the disciples of the shaykh al-Ishrâq would subsequently be known.

A famous and prolific writer, himself something of a Hermeticist (d. 291/903), makes the following observation in an essay describing the different classes of Egyptian priests: “The third class of these priests were called Ishrâqîyûn, or the children of the sister of Hermes, who is known in Greek as Hermes Trismegistus. Their parables and allegories have come down to us.” This is precisely the Hermetic ancestry that Sohrawardî repeatedly claims for himself. He regards Hermes not only as the ancestor of all wisdom, but also as the archetypal hero of mystical ecstasy (below, Chapter VI). For its part, the Islamic Hermetic tradition identifies Hermes with Idrîs, and Idrîs with the prophet Enoch.

Another equally significant piece of information appears in the commentary written by ’Abdorrazzâq Kâshânî (d. around 730/1330) on Mohyiddîn Ibn ’Arabî’s famous manual of mystical theosophy, the Fosûs al-Hikam (The Bezels of the Wisdoms of the Prophets—the “bezels” are the settings of precious stones). In that book, each prophet is contemplated not simply as belonging to a particular period in chronological history, but as embodying a degree in the hierarchy of being and wisdom.

The commentator specifies that Seth, the son of Adam, is the prophet and initiator of the Ishrâqîyûn. Among the Ishrâqîyûn, Seth is traditionally identified with Agathodaimon; in Sohrawardî’s writings the name Agathodaimon is most often mentioned together with that of Hermes. This is all the more interesting because certain ancient Gnostics, called Sethians on account of their veneration of Seth, regarded Christ as a manifestation of Seth.

Seth, moreover, was identified with Zoroaster, who in a famous prophecy identified himself with the saviour to come—“I am he, and he is I”—the Saoshyant, who would be born of his line and would one day renew the world. All these indications are rich in meaning for a phenomenology of religion that seeks to discover the intentions through which these figures “show themselves” to consciousness and through which these connections are established among them.

Finally, if we turn to a classic reference work in the Islamic world, the Book of Definitions by Sharîf Gorgânî (d. around 818/1415–1416), we read: “The Peripatetic philosophers (mashsha’ûn) are those whose master is Aristotle. The ishrâqîyûn philosophers are those whose master is Plato.” Accordingly, in the prologue to his great book Sohrawardî speaks of “the Imam of wisdom, our master Plato.”

Hermes, Zoroaster, Plato: these three great figures dominate the horizon of the Ishrâqîyûn, the “Platonists of Persia” who followed Sohrawardî. Other figures would join them, drawn from Iran’s past or chosen from among the Greek sages, who also, it was believed, drew their light from the “Niche of the Lights of Prophecy.”

Together they would make up the silsilat al-’irfân, the “sacred lineage of gnosis,” or spiritual knowledge. The spiritual perceptions and visionary ecstasies of its great figures furnished so many precedents for the Prophet of Islam’s heavenly ascent (Mi’râj). Across the centuries, the story of that ascent, in its many versions and elaborations, became an archetype for the meditation of mystical theosophers in Islam.

And when the Platonists of Islamic Persia interpreted Plato’s Ideas in terms of Zoroastrian angelology, were they not intuitively rediscovering a situation known to us through the accounts of Eudoxus of Cnidus? For Eudoxus tells us of the interest, even the enthusiasm, that prevailed in Plato’s Academy for Zarathustra. We know, moreover, from a papyrus discovered at Herculaneum listing the members of the Platonic Academy, that during Plato’s final years the Academy included a “Chaldean”—that is, an Achaemenid subject from Mesopotamia. This person may have been the source of Eudoxus’s report, and of the edifying parallels it drew between Zarathustra and Plato.

Whatever the case, Sohrawardî’s great undertaking cannot be “explained” simply by collecting its antecedents. Rather, the reverse is true: ultimately it is Sohrawardî himself, his own person, who explains how those antecedents came together. For anyone convinced that a creative intuition is not something to be explained but is itself the source and principle of explanation, no accumulation of earlier influences could ever account for the birth of such an undertaking. It is the creative intuition that first makes those earlier things its antecedents.

We can already see how Sohrawardî understood his own position from the words he uses. He treats Ishrâq (the Orient as the moment when the sun rises, the illumination of dawn) and mashriq (the Orient as a place, the land in the East) as equivalent terms. So too with Ishrâqîyûn and Mashriqîyûn (the Easterners), and with Hikmat ishrâqîya and Hikmat mashriqîya (Eastern Theosophy). His disciples and commentators, generation after generation, did the same.

Yet long before Sohrawardî—who has remained almost unknown in the West down to our own time—his illustrious predecessor Avicenna, a name familiar to Western readers for centuries through medieval Latin translations, was himself said to have conceived a project for an “Eastern” philosophy (mashriqîya).
We must therefore ask Sohrawardî himself how he understood his relationship to Avicenna, for the answer is of decisive importance to the meaning of the present book.

We have already discussed this question at some length elsewhere, both in editing the works of the shaykh al-Ishrâq and in a book on Avicenna. We do not intend to reopen the debate here. We have preferred to seek an answer in Sohrawardî’s own statements, because they seem to us far more directly relevant than the hypotheses proposed by various modern scholars.

Let us simply recall the broad outline. The question was needlessly tangled by a misreading made in the West during the nineteenth century, through ignorance of the state of philosophy in Iran, even down to our own day. Why, instead of reading mashriqîya (“Eastern”), did someone decide to read moshriqîya and give the word the meaning of “illuminative” philosophy? For many reasons, this latter word, even if theoretically possible, could never have been the name of a school of philosophers.

This was demonstrated by the famous Italian Orientalist C. Nallino in a paper published in 1925, whose arguments and conclusion everyone then contented themselves with repeating for a long time. The first misfortune was that this victorious demonstration proved what should never have been in doubt. Any Iranian shaykh teaching hikmat ilâhîya, divine wisdom, or any of his students, could have told us long ago, had anyone thought to ask, that no one in Iran had ever read the word as anything but mashriqîya, “Eastern” philosophy.

The second misfortune was that Nallino, neglecting the context of the gloss by Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî that had set him on the right path, wanted to go much further. He artificially separated the Ishrâqîyûn from the Mashriqîyûn. According to him, the former, whom he called “Illuminationists,” belonged exclusively to Sohrawardî, whereas the latter, the “Easterners,” were the philosophers Avicenna had in mind.

Now, he was right to think that Avicenna’s “Eastern” philosophy—announced in his great work, the Kitâb al-Shifâ, as the work that would contain his own philosophy—would, had it survived in full, have been something different from Sohrawardî’s ishrâqî philosophy. Without such a difference there would have been no shaykh al-Ishrâq, no distinct philosophy of Sohrawardî.

But it was wrong to declare that the Ishrâqîyûn were not Mashriqîyûn. How, indeed, could anyone make such a claim while holding the old Iranian lithographed edition of Sohrawardî’s Eastern Theosophy, where it is easy to see that both Sohrawardî and his commentators use ishrâqîyûn and mashriqîyûn interchangeably for the same idea? I can explain this insistence only as an extraordinary aversion to the Neoplatonists, especially Iamblichus and the great Proclus.

Nallino’s extreme rationalism allowed him to see nothing in the Neoplatonists but “extravagances” (sic). At all costs, heaven knows why, Avicenna had to be kept safe from such compromising company. It is true that the few surviving “notebooks” of Avicenna, believed to preserve his Logic of the Easterners, contain nothing ishrâqî in Sohrawardî’s sense.

But it would be altogether false to claim that Avicenna’s “Notes” in the margins of the so-called Theology of Aristotle—a text we now know to be a reworking of Plotinus’s Enneads—or an Avicennian mystical narrative such as the Story of the Bird, have nothing in common with Sohrawardî’s undertaking.

In short, from Sohrawardî’s point of view, and in keeping with his own statements, the situation can be summed up as follows. Avicenna wrote a large work entitled Kitâb al-Insâf wa’l-Intisâf, something like The Book of Making Just Distinctions. It was an extensive work in which he distinguished the “Easterners” from other philosophers. Unfortunately, the manuscript of this still unfinished work, which would have contained Avicenna’s “Eastern philosophy,” was lost—apart from a few fragments—during the sack of Isfahan in 1034. Avicenna did not live long enough to reconstruct it.

Sohrawardî refers, on the one hand, to fragments of this Kitâb al-Insâf, and, on the other, to scattered notebooks surviving from an incomplete and damaged whole. They contain a logic whose teachings Avicenna associated with the “Easterners.” Sohrawardî rightly observes that, despite this attribution, the notebooks contain little more than Peripatetic theses and belong to ordinary philosophy. Their authentic connection with the “Eastern source” has therefore not been established.

For Sohrawardî this is the central question. When he speaks of “Eastern philosophy,” he means the philosophy that springs from the “Eastern” teaching of the sages of ancient Persia, whom he calls the Khosrawânîyûn, for reasons we shall soon discover. His position is this: Avicenna was undoubtedly the first to attempt to establish an “Eastern” teaching distinct from Peripatetic philosophy.

But because he had no access to the “Eastern source” (asl mashriqî), he could not bring his undertaking to completion. Henceforth anyone wishing to be initiated into the philosophy and theosophy of the “Easterners” must turn to Sohrawardî himself.

This is not the place to reopen the problem of “Eastern philosophy” in Avicenna’s own writings. What concerns us is Sohrawardî’s position as a whole. For a closer examination, we can sum it up in three propositions. 1) As Sohrawardî conceived and realized it, the philosophy of Ishrâq considers itself to be Eastern philosophy. Precisely for that reason it is also a philosophy of illumination: it prepares the soul to receive “Eastern flashes,” the archangelic Lights that “rise and shed their light” upon it. It provides the ontological and phenomenological foundation for this “Eastern” experience—that is, an account of its reality and of how it reveals itself.

As we shall see again, it is “illuminative” because it is “Eastern,” and “Eastern” because it is “illuminative.” This is the true relationship, in Sohrawardî’s thought, between the meanings carried by the two terms Ishrâq and mashriq. 2) Avicenna’s idea of the Orient and Sohrawardî’s idea of the Orient have something in common insofar as the Orient is understood in its true sense: metaphysically, not geographically.

In Avicenna, this Orient appears in the Story of Hayy ibn Yaqzân, in the commentary on the Verse of Light (Qur’an 24:35), in the Story of the Bird, and in references found in the “Notes” written in the margins of the so-called Theology of Aristotle. In Sohrawardî, it is the Orient understood as the universe of archangelic Lights, arising from the “Light of Glory” (Xvarnah) and surrounding the Light of Lights with a radiance, with all the Orients that form its ascending degrees.

But 3) there is a profound difference in what each personally accomplished as a spiritual realization. Sohrawardî expresses it most clearly in the prologue to his Story of the Western Exile (below, Chapter VI). And the shaykh al-Ishrâq knew perfectly well the reasons for this difference. To bring the “Eastern source” back to life—the teachings and symbols of the sages of ancient Persia—was his own work, an undertaking in which he had no predecessor, since Avicenna, not knowing that source, had been unable to complete his.

He expresses this conviction repeatedly, for example in a treatise devoted specifically to Sufism. Sohrawardî writes: “Among the ancient Persians (fî’l-Fors) there was a community of men guided by God (al-Haqq) who therefore walked upon the straight path, eminent sages possessed of divine wisdom, unlike the Magi (Majûs). It is their precious theosophy of Light—the very wisdom witnessed in the mystical experience of Plato and his predecessors—that we have revived in our book entitled Eastern Theosophy. And in pursuing such an undertaking I had no forerunner.”

A passage like this widens the scope of our inquiry still further. Brief though it is, it has the force of a manifesto. It states the author's purpose plainly: to bring back to life the wisdom, or theosophy, taught in ancient Persia by a group of sages whose teachings and spiritual life were in harmony with those of Plato and the early Greek sages.

Two features tell us precisely what kind of sages these ancient Persians were. To establish the first, the shaykh al-Ishrâq—the Master of Illumination—uses ta’wîl, an interpretive reading that brings different moments of sacred history into relation.

A verse of the Quran says: “Among the people of Moses there was a community of men who were guided by God and followed the straight path” (7:159). Through this interpretive transposition, Sohrawardî applies to the sages of ancient Persia what the Quran says about a chosen group among the people of Moses.

The second feature completes the first. Because these Persian sages were guided by God, Sohrawardî is careful not to let them be confused with those commonly called the Majûs. In both Persian and Arabic, this is the usual name for the “Magi,” the followers of the ancient Iranian religion.
But how are we to reconcile these claims? At the very moment when Sohrawardî affirms his spiritual descent from the sages of ancient Persia, he expressly rejects the impiety of the “Magi.”

Yet for us, historically, that name designates the bearers of Iran's ancient Mazdean wisdom—the very wisdom Sohrawardî wishes to “resurrect.” What are we to make of this? The question matters, because the entire meaning of Sohrawardî's undertaking depends on the answer.

Put simply, the Magi whom Sohrawardî rejects are those who professed a radical dualism: the belief that the two Principles, Light and Darkness, have existed eternally alongside one another. This is not the doctrine he intended to revive.

We shall see later how he explains the metaphysical meaning of the opposition symbolized by these two Principles. His account agrees with what we learn from Shahrastânî (d. 1153), that outstanding early historian of religions.

Shahrastânî's account can be summed up in three points. 1) The Magi (Majûs) are the radical dualists. 2) The original Magi (al-Majûs al-aslîya), however, did not teach that two distinct Principles were equally eternal in their very being.

They differed instead over how Darkness came into existence, while preserving the primacy of Light. 3) Zoroaster himself belonged to these original Magi. They held that Light and Darkness came from one Principle, but “explained” evil as the result of Darkness becoming mixed with Light.

Zoroaster could thus be understood as another prophet of the One God, who has no partner, opposite, or equal. The outlines of Zoroaster's teaching found in Shahrastânî, in Sohrawardî, and much later in Qotboddîn Ashkevârî, a disciple of Mîr Dâmâd in the seventeenth century, agree with one another.
This picture of Zoroaster, the prophet of ancient Persia, and of his Magi presupposes a whole history of religious developments, above all the steady westward movement of Zoroastrian Magianism.
From Bactria, at the far eastern edge of the Iranian world, Zoroastrianism in its Sasanian and post-Sasanian forms came to be established in the western Iranian lands.
Zoroaster himself then came to be thought of as a native of Azerbaijan. The sacred geography of the Avesta was reversed, as though it had turned around an imaginary axis.
Yet this was only one stage of the movement “westward,” one part of a larger pattern whose coherence some future phenomenological study might reveal.

That study would have to follow the successive rebirths of Zoroaster and his Magi in human consciousness, asking in each case what conditions of consciousness made these figures appear as they did—from the great Byzantine reformer George Gemistos Plethon in the fifteenth century, all the way to Friedrich Nietzsche.

Although we can deal with these matters only in broad outline, we must recall a series of developments of enormous importance for the religious destiny of humanity. From its base in the western part of the Iranian world, Zoroastrian Magianism spread farther west along two routes.

One route ran southwest, toward Chaldea. Had Babylon not long served as the Great King's winter residence? The encounter with Chaldean wisdom gave rise to what we may call Magian-Chaldeanism, which passed through Syria to Alexandria. That city had become an intellectual center of Hellenism and, more immediately important to us, a center of Neoplatonism.
A shared religious and philosophical passion among kindred minds made possible an encounter between Platonism, Orphism, Hermeticism, and Magian-Chaldean thought.

The echoes of that encounter can still be heard in Sohrawardî's work, within Islam. It was from this spiritual setting that the famous text known as the Oracula chaldaïca, or Chaldean Oracles, emerged.

Gemistos Plethon, and probably others before him, attributed these oracles to Zoroaster. In fact, they were composed in the second half of the second century by two devout theosophers: Julian the Chaldean and his son, Julian the Theurgist.

Written in an obscure symbolic language, the Chaldean Oracles—“Chaldean” here being a rather loose ethnic designation—concern the knowledge of noetic beings: beings of the intelligible world who govern our own. The means of communicating with them are likewise noetic, that is, spiritual.

The text profoundly influenced the Neoplatonist philosophers. Iamblichus, Syrianus, Proclus, and others wrote extensive commentaries on it, treating its difficult sayings almost as though they belonged to a sacred scripture.

As these Neoplatonists understood and contemplated them—and we shall return to them in a few pages when discussing Sohrawardî's vocabulary—the Oracula, or Logia, present something like a “Hellenized Magianism.”

Yet this Magianism, fashioned by Neoplatonists drawn toward the East, no longer teaches the radical dualism of the Majûs, the Magi condemned by Sohrawardî. It accords instead with the picture of Zoroaster as a prophet of the One God, and with Shahrastânî's understanding of the “original Magi.”
Sohrawardî will prefer to call these sages the Khosrawânîyûn; we shall see why.

The other route led northwest, through Asia Minor—to Armenia, Pontus, and Cappadocia. The Magi of Asia Minor are commonly known as the Maguseans. They certainly acknowledged Zoroaster as the founder of their rites and mysteries, but Zurvanite doctrine predominated among them.

At the same time, Mithra and the mysteries devoted to him took the central place. In the Avesta, by contrast, Mithra is only one of the Yazatas, the divine beings created by Ahura Mazda, the “Lord Wisdom.”
As we know, the mysteries of Mithra eventually spread throughout the Roman Empire, reaching Britain, Gaul, and Spain.

Sadly, only the remains of monuments and fragments of ravaged literatures allow us to trace this extraordinary expansion of Iranian Magianism. Hermippus, a celebrated librarian of the great library of Alexandria, not only wrote a multivolume work On the Magi.

According to Pliny, he also compiled a catalogue of writings attributed to Zoroaster—or, more precisely, to the Magi of his school: works placed under his authority because they had been composed in the spirit of his teaching.

Altogether, they amounted to two million lines: an entire library in itself. Only scattered fragments and passing references survive. The Oracula chaldaïca mentioned above must have formed part of that literature.

But it has taken the immense labor of patient scholars to recover what remains of them—some four hundred verses, preserved as quotations scattered through the surviving writings of the Neoplatonist philosophers.

As for the Magi of Mithra, the Maguseans of Asia Minor, we owe to Dio Chrysostom (second century) a passage from their psalter: one of the hymns which, he tells us, “Zoroaster and the children of the Magi sang, having learned it from him.”
In this hymn, Zoroastrian teachings mingle with Stoic ideas. It tells the symbolic story of the cosmic chariot and its four horses, representing the four Elements.

We find something similar in the four pillars of the Throne described by Islamic gnostics, who had themselves learned, by one route or another, of the tetramorph—the fourfold figure in Ezekiel’s vision.
We shall also have occasion later to recall the text known as the “Liturgy of Mithra.”
Faced with so many losses, so much accumulated ruin, scholars of religion remain inconsolable even today.
But Sohrawardî's response was characteristic of the man. He would not be content simply to mourn. He would be a “resurrector,” one who brings a lost wisdom back to life.

And we see him setting about the task, certain of his path, once he has cleared away the misunderstanding concerning those Magi whose radical dualism had made them unfaithful to the true teaching of the ancient Persian sages.
His own spiritual experience will appeal to the testimony of Zoroaster's visions: visions of the blazing Light of Glory, of the Lights of the divine Heptad, and so on.

Now, in the “hieratic ascent” described by the Chaldean Oracles, the same imagery of Light and Fire predominates: the hymn of Fire, the flower of Fire, the paths of Fire, the most holy living Fire worshipped in the silence of the soul's sanctuary.
We may also sense an echo of the psalter of the Magi of Mithra in the hymns that Sohrawardî addressed to the Angel of the Sun and to the “Perfect Nature” (see below, III, 5).

Throughout his writings, in other words, we find scattered features of the same kind as those which led certain Neoplatonists, and later Gemistos Plethon, to recognize an affinity between the Chaldean Oracles and the theosophy of Zoroaster's Magi. It was the same intuition that led the Byzantine philosopher to bring the names of Plato and Zoroaster together.

We may even wonder whether his teacher, the mysterious Jew Elisha—who introduced him to the name of Zoroaster and was said to have been a disciple of Averroes—was not, rather, a wandering ishrâqî who had found his way to Anatolia.
Three centuries before Gemistos Plethon, Sohrawardî had already brought the names and teachings of Plato and Zoroaster together within Islam.

But the Byzantine and the Iranian philosophers pursued their work in very different circumstances. Through Gemistos Plethon, the “Hellenized Magi” would be carried still farther west, to his friends in the Platonic Academy of Florence.

Plethon's aim was to place a great philosophical and religious reform under Zoroaster's patronage: a religion of the future that would overcome, and make people forget, the antagonism between the religion of Christ and the religion of Muhammad.

Our shaykh al-Ishrâq, by contrast, feels no such opposition that must be overcome. For him, the spiritual resources of Islamic gnosis itself—hikmat and ’irfân, wisdom and mystical knowledge—make it possible to bring about the rebirth of the sages of ancient Persia.
Seen in this light, Sohrawardî's work completes a magnificent circuit that began with the two migrations of Magianism to the southwest and northwest.

It is as though Zoroaster's Magi, having clothed themselves during their westward travels in Chaldean wisdom and the Platonism of the Neoplatonists drawn toward the East, now needed Sohrawardî to bring them home to Persia—but to the Islamic Persia of the twelfth century, carrying all the treasures of mystical theosophy that their disciples had gathered under their inspiration.

To bring them home was, above all, to reconnect this Platonizing Magianism with the Avestan tradition, of which Sohrawardî certainly knew a few authentic fragments—those concerning the xvarnah, the Light of Glory, and the world of angels—and with the heroic traditions of ancient Iran, preserved within Islamic Persia by Ferdawsî's Shâh-Nâmeh, the Book of Kings.

Through this rebirth, the heroic epic of ancient Iran begins to unfold as a mystical epic. It will be one of the most compelling aspects of the shaykh al-Ishrâq's vast and intricate work (see Chapter V below).

What sustains him is his sense of belonging to a spiritual family scattered across the earth, yet bound together by an invisible, unbreakable bond, as closely united as the branches of a single great tree. It is the great tree of Wisdom, whose branches never cease to grow and spread, nourished by a mysterious sap.

Sohrawardî gives this sap the form of an “Eternal Leaven,” a living ferment that passes mystically from spirit to spirit. No “sufficient reason” drawn from history can explain its movement if we look only at the machinery of demonstrable causes.
Strengthened by the certainty of his spiritual ancestry, by his gratitude for it, and by the duty it lays upon him, he can devote himself to his work as a “resurrector.”
Thus he writes: “We have entrusted the knowledge of True Reality to our book entitled Theosophy of the Orient.

“In it we have revived the ancient wisdom that the Imams of India, Persia (Fârs), Chaldea, and Egypt, and those of the ancient Greeks down to Plato, always took as their central point of reference, drawing from it their own theosophy. This wisdom is the Eternal Leaven (al-Khamîrat al-azalîya).”

It is this idea of the Leaven, like sap spreading through the branches of the tree of Wisdom, that leads Sohrawardî, on the final pages of his Crossroads and Conversations, to sketch the spiritual “family tree” of the Ishrâqîyûn, the philosophers of Illumination.
The outward opposition between Greek sages and “Eastern” sages disappears. Both are “guardians of the Logos” (Kalimat), one group on the “western side,” the other on the “eastern side.”
Sohrawardî's account allows us to picture this family tree as follows. At its root stands Hermes, the father of the sages. From him imagine two great branches.

On the “eastern side” stand the ancient Persian sages (the Pahlawîyûn): Gayomart, the primordial king, followed by two heroes whose deeds, belonging to an age before Zarathustra or Zoroaster, are already celebrated in the Avesta—the sacred kings Fereydûn and Kay Khosraw.

The ecstatic sages who came after them were called Khosrawânîyûn, after Kay Khosraw (see Chapter IV below). Sohrawardî sees their spiritual leaven reaching him through three Sufi masters: Abû Yazîd Bastâmî (the “wanderer” of Bastâm), Mansûr Hallâj (the fatâ, or “knight,” of Bayza), and Abû’l-Hasan Kharraqânî (the wanderer of Amâl and Kharraqân).
On the “western side” stand Asclepius, Empedocles, Pythagoras, and Plato. The leaven of the Pythagoreans then passes into Islam through Akhî Akhmîm (Dhû’l-Nûn Misrî) and Abû Sahl Tostarî.
At last the two sides come together, like the curved branches of a cypress meeting at its crown, in a community of spiritual seekers whose speech becomes the instrument of the Sakîna.

This last word calls for a long explanation. For Sohrawardî, its meaning reaches back to one of the most fundamental Zoroastrian ideas he brought back to life: that of the luminous Presence, the Light of Glory, the Xvarnah (see Chapter III below).
Here, too, we find the spiritual ancestry that, in Sohrawardî's thought and experience, links the mystics of Islam to the mystical theosophers of ancient Persia.

Let us gather a few essential points. For Sohrawardî and the mystics close to him, the Sakîna is above all the experience of a Presence made known by a sign, or by signs. These are not perceived through our ordinary physical senses, but through “spiritual senses” able to perceive the intermediate, or imaginal, world.
